{{Short description|Population census conducted in Armenia}}
'''Census in Armenia''' is a population census conducted in [[Armenia]] about every 10 years with the purpose of capturing exact data on [[Demographics of Armenia|demographics in the country]].

== Demographic trends ==
While [[Armenians]] formed a consistent majority, [[Azerbaijani people|Azerbaijanis]] were historically the second largest population in the republic under [[Armenian SSR|Soviet rule]] (forming about 2.5% in 1989<ref name="1989census">{{in lang|ru}} [http://demoscope.ru/weekly/ssp/sng_nac_89.php?reg=13 The All-Union Population Census of 1989] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120104081804/http://demoscope.ru/weekly/ssp/sng_nac_89.php?reg=13 |date=January 4, 2012 }}. ''Demoscope.ru''</ref>).  However, due to hostilities with neighboring Azerbaijan over the disputed region of [[Nagorno-Karabakh]] virtually all Azeris emigrated from Armenia.  Conversely, Armenia received a large influx of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan, thus giving Armenia a more homogeneous character.  This forceful population exchange also affected the Christian [[Udi people]] of Azerbaijan, many of whom were perceived as Armenians due to close cultural ties between both peoples.<ref name="udis">{{cite news
  | title = Muslim Kurds and Christian Udis
  | publisher = Hetq Online
  | date = 2006-11-13
  | url = http://www.hetq.am/eng/society/0611-udis.html
  | access-date = 2006-11-13
  | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061116101854/http://www.hetq.am/eng/society/0611-udis.html
  | archive-date = 2006-11-16
  | url-status = dead
  }}</ref>  The number of Udis residing in Armenia has increased from 19 in 1989<ref name="1989census" /> to about 200 by 2006.<ref name="udis" />

Additionally since independence, several other ethnic groups have emigrated especially [[Russians]] (who decreased from 51,555 persons in 1989<ref name="1989census" /> to 14,660 in 2001<ref name="2001census">[http://docs.armstat.am/census/pdfs/51.pdf Information from the 2001 Armenian National Census]</ref>), [[Ukrainians]] (8,341 in 1989<ref name="1989census" /> to 1,633 in 2001<ref name="2001census" />), [[Greeks]] (4,650 in 1989<ref name="1989census" /> to 1,176 in 2001<ref name="2001census" />), and [[Belarusians]] (1,061 in 1989<ref name="1989census" /> to 160 in 2001<ref name="minorities">Garnik Asatryan and Victoria Arakelova, ''[http://www.osce.org/documents/oy/2002/01/148_en.pdf The Ethnic Minorities of Armenia] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070710071814/http://www.osce.org/documents/oy/2002/01/148_en.pdf |date=July 10, 2007 }}'', Routledge, part of the [[Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe|OSCE]], 2002</ref>).  The numbers of [[Yazidis]], [[Kurdish people|Kurds]], and [[Assyrian people|Assyrians]] have remained consistent for the most part (though approximately 2,000 Assyrians have left Armenia between 1989<ref name="1989census" /> and 2001<ref name="2001census" />). Although [[Georgians]] were historically counted among the largest ethnic groups in modern Armenia, their numbers have dropped substantially since the 1989 Soviet census when they numbered 1,364 persons.<ref name="1989census" />

==Republic of Armenia censuses==
{{Update|section|date=January 2024}}
The first census in Armenia after the [[History of the Soviet Union (1985–1991)#Yeltsin and the dissolution of the USSR|dissolution of the Soviet Union]] was conducted by the [[Government of Armenia]]'s [[Statistical Committee of Armenia|National Statistical Service]] during the period of October 10–19, 2001. The census night was October 10. The [[National Assembly (Armenia)|National Assembly]] adopted the law "On Census" in 1999, but the government lacked the necessary funds to carry out the count immediately. According to Armenian law, a census must take place every 10 years.
